items.title: 30.7.3 Determining the Structure of a Molecule from 13C NMR

source_refs.note: Topic 30.7.3 with Quick Check 30.7, answered (PDF 213-214); Figure 30.8 is redrawn. The book's conclusion (2-methoxypropane) is reported, with a warning that the printed shifts fit 2-methylpropan-1-ol. Exercises (PDF 214-216) excluded; answers need review.

items: Count the peaks: the number of peaks is the number of carbon environments. A molecule with 5 carbon atoms but only 3 peaks must have 2 pairs of chemically equivalent carbons.
Look at the position of each peak (its chemical shift) to tell whether the carbon is in an alkane, alkene, alkyne, aromatic or carbonyl environment (Table 30.3).
Work out possible structures that fit both the peak information and the molecular formula.

blocks.text: Example: a compound C4H10O gives a 13C spectrum with 3 peaks, at 69.0, 30.5 and 19.0 ppm (Figure 30.8), so there are three carbon environments. Butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol each have four different carbons and would show four peaks, so neither fits. The compound is 2-methoxypropane, which has three carbon environments.

blocks.alt: Top: horizontal bars on a 220 to 0 ppm scale for the 13C shift ranges of Table 30.3, from C=O of aldehydes and ketones (190-220) to alkyl carbon (0-50). Bottom left: a sketch of the 13C spectrum of ethanol, lines at 57 ppm (CH2) and 18 ppm (CH3). Bottom right: the three lines of Figure 30.8 at 69.0, 30.5 and 19.0 ppm.
blocks.caption: 13C chemical shift ranges, ethanol, and the unknown of Figure 30.8 (original diagram after Table 30.3 and Figures 30.7 and 30.8).
blocks.long_description: Each different carbon environment gives one unsplit line. Carbons bonded to oxygen appear at 50-70 ppm, and carbonyl carbons much further left. Counting the lines gives the number of carbon environments.

items: Using Figure 30.8, explain why the spectrum does not match butan-1-ol or butan-2-ol.
Which peaks would you expect in the spectra of butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol?
